member.summary: The Demo3D.VehicleFramework is an implementation of a vehicle movement system for Demo3D. It is coded entirely in C# as a Demo3D catalog. It is designed to be optimized for simulation, and to automatically upgrade models. These are the Demo3D.VehicleFramework namespaces.
member.remarks:
C# Design Approach Here are some of the approaches used in the design of the C# class structure.
Interfaces
Interfaces are used extensively to maintain a separation between an intended API and the implementation.
Aspects
Aspects were introduced into the Demo3D.Visuals.Visual class to support extensions like the vehicle framework. For example, vehicles are defined to be visuals that have the IVehicle aspect, and control points are defined to be visuals that have the IControlPoint aspect.
Signals
Signals were also introduced into the core of the Demo3D framework to support functional behaviour related to events produced by the framework. For example, this a signal for idle vehicles passing a control point: var idleVehicles = controlPoint.PassSignal.KeepIf( e => e.Vehicle.JobModule().IsLookingForWork )
Vehicle Framework Concepts The following explains the basic concepts used in the vehicle framework, and its theory of operation.
Vehicles
Every vehicle is an implementation of the interface IVehicle. A vehicle is something that moves from one part of the model to another, and not necessarily on a (predefined) track. If a vehicle is not attached to a track then it is considered to be driving along a temporary track, made from the passable spaces between obstacles. In that sense, it is still driving on a track. A vehicle may have its own onboard motor, or it may be driven by the track itself. For example, AGVs and trucks have their own motor, and a power & free carrier is driven by the track. A vehicle may have its own onboard motor, or it may be driven by the track itself. For example, AGVs and trucks have their own motor, and a power & free carrier is driven by the track.
Track
A track can be built from interconnected track segments. These are visuals with Demo3D.VehicleFramework.NativeObjects.TrackSegment as their native object. Track may merge, split and connect back to itself to create loops. Track sections may include speed and direction constraints. Track is connected using Demo3D connectors.
Track System
The TrackSystem is a combination of two visuals. The main parent visual's native object implements ITransferVehicleController, and it has two basic jobs. The first is to compile the track segments into an ITrackSystem, and the second is to provide basic job dispatching. The second visual is a child, and contains default logic for vehicle behaviour. The logic component implements the ITransferVehicleLogic. Originally, it was intended that ITransferVehicleController would communicate with ITransferVehicleLogic for all events, but over time the associated logic component installs listeners for the events that it is interested in, and so requires less assistance from the main controller than originally intended.
Control Points
Control points can be added to a track to detect vehicle events. A control point can be configured to detect events from one direction only. See section below on what control point events can be detected.
Motor Controllers
For Power & Free type systems, motor controllers can be attached to the track to define the various sections of driven track, along with speed and direction.
Lifts & Shuttles
Lifts and shuttles are implemented as movable track sections. The framework includes support for defining and operating lifts and shuttles.
Collision Detection
All collisions are calculated as future events using equations of motion, taking into account relative speed and acceleration.
Accumulation
By default, all vehicles will accumulate automatically. Control flags are used on the vehicle to detect vehicle presence and inhibit motion accordingly.
Route Finding
All routes are calculated using the A* path finding algorithm. Certain track sections may be given higher weightings to influence the way routes are found. By default, the route finder automatically gives a high weighting to track sections that contain stationary vehicles, so that detours can be found. In addition, control points are available that can force a recalculation so that changes in weighting, vehicle location etc can be accounted for when getting closer to a target.
Catalog
The framework is contained entirely in a catalog, and is written in C#. The catalog is versioned, so that newer releases of the catalog can automatically update existing models.

member.summary:
Interface for vehicles that can be recharged. The vehicle framework will look for aspects of this type on a vehicle and then automatically discharge the vehicle while driving, and attempt to dispatch recharging jobs when idle.
The charge rate used in this interface is a "C-rate" (see https://batteryuniversity.com/learn/article/what_is_the_c_rate). A value of 1 for C-rate (named "crate" in the interface) means that the battery will recharge from empty to full in 1 hour. A value of 2 for C-rate means the batter will recharge from empty to full in 30 mins. Therefore, a full recharge will take (60 / crate) minutes.
The rate of discharge depends on the base implementation of IChargeSystem that is chosen. The framework currently includes one simple implementation for discharging linearly based on distance travelled (see for example usage)
